meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'All religion, my friend, is simply evolved out of fraud, fear, greed, imagination, and poetry'?
meta.ogDescription: Not verifiably Poe. The line traces to a secondhand anecdote in a 1901 biography widely judged unreliable, and the original says “chicanery,” not “fraud.”

answer.label: Not verifiably Poe — a secondhand 1901 anecdote
answer.authorDates: 1809–1849 · American writer, poet, editor & literary critic
answer.sourceLine: No Poe tale, poem, essay or letter is known to contain this line. It traces to Colonel John A. Joyce’s 1901 biography Edgar Allan Poe, where Joyce repeats what a “Mr. William Barton” told him Poe said over wine. Poe scholars regard that book as unreliable, and Joyce’s text reads “chicanery,” not “fraud.” Quote Investigator ↗ calls its authenticity doubtful.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Colonel John A. Joyce (1842–1915), biographer, not Poe
F. T. Neely Co., New York, 1901, p. 108

source.excerpt:
“‘Mr. Poe, what do you think of the religions of the world?’
‘From the earliest dawn of creation man has worshipped something — sticks, stones, snakes, stars, suns, mountains, rivers, seas, myths, calves, popes and preachers. He is largely an ape and mimics anything with glitter, pomp and power. …
‘No man who ever lived knows any more about the hereafter, Barton, than you and I, and all religion, my friend, is simply evolved out of chicanery, fear, greed, imagination and poetry!’”
trail: 1901: Colonel John A. Joyce’s biography Edgar Allan Poe prints the remark as something William Barton, described as a typo and foreman at the Broadway Journal, told him Poe said. Scan at the Internet Archive ↗
1906: Rufus K. Noyes reprints it in his quotation collection Views of Religion, misspelling the name as “Edgar Allen Poe.” Quote Investigator ↗
1996: James A. Haught’s 2000 Years of Disbelief runs a shortened version with ellipses, credited “Poe (Noyes).” Quote Investigator ↗
2012–2017: The World of Edgar Allan Poe blog calls the quote apocryphal (2012). Quote Investigator then concludes the evidence is secondhand and the biography is not credible (2017). World of Poe ↗
source.excerptNote: Joyce sets this up as a conversation Barton reported to him: “Mr. Barton told me this.” Joyce printed “chicanery.” The popular “fraud” version is a later variant with no known source.

source.rightsNote: The only documented text of the line is John A. Joyce’s biography Edgar Allan Poe, published in New York in 1901. Works first published before 1931 are in the U.S. public domain. The modern “fraud” variant is an anonymous one-word change to that text, with no known source of its own.

author.heading: Who Poe actually was
author.metaLine: 1809–1849 · American writer, poet, editor & literary critic
author.bio: Edgar Allan Poe (January 19, 1809 – October 7, 1849) was, in Wikipedia’s words, an American writer, poet, editor, and literary critic. He worked as an editor of the Broadway Journal and later owned it; the journal failed in 1846. Joyce’s anecdote is set in that job. The line is not known from any of Poe’s own writings, and every source Quote Investigator traces leads back to Joyce’s secondhand report.

misattribution.heading: Why it gets pinned on Poe
misattribution.intro: The line has a real paper trail, but it starts with a secondhand anecdote in a much-criticized biography, not with Poe. Freethought anthologies then repeated it, and somewhere along the way “chicanery” became “fraud.”

items.why: No Poe writing is known to contain the line. Joyce’s 1901 biography reports it secondhand, and Quote Investigator notes that Poe enthusiasts consider the book unreliable and doubt the quotation. Quote Investigator ↗
Joyce names Barton as his source. The World of Edgar Allan Poe blog says it found no other sign that Barton existed and calls the quote apocryphal. World of Poe, 2012 ↗
Joyce’s text reads “chicanery, fear, greed, imagination and poetry.” Wikiquote lists the line under Disputed and notes that it is “sometimes quoted” with “fraud.” Wikiquote ↗

items.who: Rufus K. Noyes (1906) and James A. Haught (1996)
items.why: Two freethought quotation collections reprinted the line under Poe’s name, which carried Joyce’s anecdote into later anthologies. Quote Investigator ↗

misattribution.truthLine: The line goes back to John A. Joyce’s 1901 biography Edgar Allan Poe (p. 108), which says “chicanery,” not “fraud,” and presents it as Barton’s recollection, not Poe’s writing. Quote Investigator calls its authenticity doubtful. Read the passage ↗

context.heading: Why the source matters
lead: Joyce’s biography is the problem at the root of this quote. The World of Edgar Allan Poe blog calls it a “justifiably obscure 1901 biography” full of “outlandish and clearly fictional statements.” Its example is Joyce’s chapter claiming that “The Raven” was stolen from a poem called “The Parrot” that the blogger says never existed. World of Poe ↗

Even read at face value, Joyce’s passage is a memory twice removed. Barton tells Joyce what Poe said one night when both were “mellowed with the fumes of the wine cup.” Quote Investigator says plainly that it lacks the subject expertise to rule on the quote’s accuracy. What can be documented is the chain: Joyce in 1901, then quotation anthologies, then the internet’s “fraud” version.
context.pull: A memory twice removed: Barton’s account, as told to Joyce.

sourcesVerified.claim: The remark appeared in Colonel John A. Joyce's 1901 Poe biography, reported secondhand from William Barton. Poe aficionados consider the biography unreliable. It was reprinted by Noyes (1906, 'Allen' misspelling) and Haught (1996, with ellipses). QI lacks the expertise to evaluate its accuracy.

Wikiquote lists 'All religion, my friend, is simply evolved out of chicanery…' under Disputed, notes it is sometimes quoted with 'fraud', and attributes it to Joyce's much-criticized 1901 biography, where Barton is the reported source.

Joyce, Edgar Allan Poe (F.T. Neely Co., 1901; Joyce 1842–1915) contains the Barton anecdote, with the line 'all religion, my friend, is simply evolved out of chicanery, fear, greed, imagination and poetry!' on p. 108.

The World of Edgar Allan Poe blog (May 21, 2012) calls the quote apocryphal, calls Joyce's 1901 biography full of fictional statements (including 'The Parrot' claim), and says it found no other sign that Barton existed.
Poe (Jan 19, 1809 – Oct 7, 1849) was an American writer, poet, editor and literary critic, and was editor and later owner of the Broadway Journal, which failed in 1846.
